title: India Plans National Framework to Keep Older Workers in the Workforce and Build Dementia-Inclusive Communities
excerpt: The Bureau of Indian Standards is drafting guidelines that would help organizations create age-inclusive workplaces as India's 60-plus population heads toward 230 million by 2036.
body:
• India's Bureau of Indian Standards is developing a national framework to promote greater workforce participation among people aged 60 and above, alongside quality-of-care protocols.
  • India's elderly population is projected to more than double from 100 million in 2011 to 230 million by 2036, with the UNFPA estimating 346 million by 2050.
  • A key element of the framework addresses dementia, with cases projected to nearly double from 8.8 million to 17 million by 2036.
  • The National Career Service portal has already identified 168,000 job vacancies suitable for candidates aged over 60.

India is preparing a national framework aimed at keeping older citizens economically active and building communities equipped to support people living with dementia, according to two government officials familiar with the initiative.

The Bureau of Indian Standards, which operates under the department of consumer affairs, has been tasked with developing the framework. It will establish protocols for the quality of care for older persons and lay out guidelines for organizations to create age-inclusive workplaces, the officials told Mint on condition of anonymity.

A Demographic Shift India Cannot Ignore

The urgency is demographic. India's population aged 60 and above is projected to rise from 100 million in 2011 to 230 million by 2036, increasing their share of the population from 8.4% to 14.9%, according to federal policy think tank NITI Aayog. The United Nations Population Fund projects an even sharper long-term trajectory, estimating that 346 million Indians — nearly 21% of the population — could be over 60 by 2050.

https://x.com/livemint/status/2096572275147637111

The shift is already reshaping how families function. HelpAge India's 2026 research found that among older people living alone, 38% depended on neighbours for care, 20% relied on family members living elsewhere, and 16% received no care at all.

Keeping Older Workers Active

The proposed framework would move India beyond viewing its elderly population as care recipients and instead position them as a continuing economic force. Half of male senior citizens and 22% of female senior citizens are already working, according to NITI Aayog's 2024 Senior Care Reforms paper, which cites the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India.

"The government is working on a draft on creating an age-inclusive workforce, with general requirements and guidelines for organizations to address the needs of an ageing workforce," one official said. "The idea is to help organizations create a work environment that is inclusive of people across different age groups and is responsive to the needs of an ageing workforce."

There are already signs of demand. Union minister for social justice and empowerment Virendra Kumar told the Rajya Sabha in July that the National Career Service portal had identified 168,000 vacancies as suitable for candidates aged above 60.

Tackling Dementia at Community Level

Another pillar of the proposed framework targets dementia — not just as a medical condition, but as a community planning challenge. The number of Indians aged 60 and above living with dementia is projected to nearly double from an estimated 8.8 million in 2026 to about 17 million by 2036, according to a social justice ministry document. The prevalence rate among the elderly stands at 7.4%.

The framework would promote dementia-inclusive communities, moving the issue beyond clinical care to how neighbourhoods, public spaces, and local institutions accommodate people living with the condition.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For millions of NRIs with aging parents in India, the framework could address a persistent anxiety: who provides care when family is thousands of miles away. India currently has 705 government-supported senior citizen homes, but the government has signalled it will follow international practices that extend care beyond institutions to home-based services.

"We need to look at older people not just as recipients of care but as an economically active section of society. Creating opportunities for them to remain engaged in the workforce, along with ensuring quality care and support for families and caregivers, can help address these emerging needs."

— D.P. Majhi, former director of Dr Ambedkar Foundation

What to Watch

The BIS framework remains in draft stage, with no timeline announced for its release. India's unemployment rate stood at 5.1% in July, with an estimated 566 million people aged 15 and above employed during April–June 2026, according to the Periodic Labour Force Survey. How the framework balances the needs of an aging workforce against youth employment pressures will be a key test of the policy's design.
